edition.sessionCovered: Fri, Nov 13 (BTC crashes below $70K — $1.3B liquidated · Gold $3,888 as PPI tame · Silver one-year low $48.65 · Brent $95.84 · Anthropic IPO Nov 19)
edition.fomc: Next: 8–9 Dec (25bp hike near certain; ~10% odds of 50bp)
edition.stripNote: Sat 14 Nov. Bitcoin crashed below $70,000 on Friday the 13th, falling 5.1% to approximately $68,300 — over $1.3 billion in crypto liquidations within 24 hours; Fear & Greed Index collapsed to 20 ('Extreme Fear'). Gold stabilized near $3,888 after tame October PPI (+0.3% MoM, +6.5% YoY, below the 6.6% consensus). Silver plunged 2.6% to $48.65, a one-year low. Brent settled flat at $95.84; WTI $88.30 (−0.5%). The 10-year yield rose to 5.15%; dollar index hit 103.4. Grains rebounded: wheat +1.6% to 593½¢, corn +0.8% to 446¢, soybeans +1.1% to 1,233¢. S&P 7,561.67 (−0.4%), Dow 52,347.55 (+0.1%), Nasdaq 25,136.27 (−0.9%) — but Wall Street notched a winning week. Nvidia $162.69 (−2%), down ~$600B in market cap for the week after Jensen Huang's resignation. Anthropic targets Nasdaq debut Nov 19 under ticker ANT at up to $2T valuation, IPO reportedly 6x oversubscribed. The Washington Institute counted 37 ship attacks in Hormuz in October, the highest monthly total since the war began. The Nov 27 gallium/germanium/antimony deadline is 13 days away.

overview: Friday's session was defined by a brutal crypto sell-off and divergent commodity moves as markets digested October's slightly tamer PPI report. Bitcoin crashed below $70,000 for the first time since August, plunging 5.1% to approximately $68,300 and triggering over $1.3 billion in crypto liquidations within 24 hours. The Fear and Greed Index collapsed to 20 — 'Extreme Fear' — its lowest reading since July. Ethereum fell 3.2% to approximately $1,930, slipping below $2,000 for the first time since August. The sell-off was amplified by Anthropic's upcoming IPO — reportedly six times oversubscribed at up to $2 trillion valuation, with pricing targeted for November 18 and trading on November 19 — which analysts said was draining liquidity as investors raised cash for allocations. Gold stabilized near $3,888, up 0.3%, finding bargain-hunting support after Thursday's 2.8% plunge, though it posted its steepest weekly loss of 2026. The October PPI came in at 0.3% month-over-month and 6.5% year-over-year — slightly below the 6.6% consensus — but failed to dent December rate-hike expectations. The 10-year Treasury yield rose to 5.15%, and the dollar index climbed to 103.4. Brent settled essentially flat at $95.84 after Trump reiterated the US does not need a deal with Iran. The S&P 500 closed at 7,561.67 (−0.4%), the Dow at 52,347.55 (+0.1%), and the Nasdaq at 25,136.27 (−0.9%) — led lower by AMD (−8.8%) and Broadcom (−4.8%). Nvidia closed at $162.69 (−2%), shedding approximately $600 billion in market capitalisation for the week since Jensen Huang's resignation.

Silver was Friday's standout loser among traditional commodities, falling 2.6% to $48.65 — a new one-year low — as its industrial-demand profile wilted alongside the AI sector sell-off. The gold-to-silver ratio widened to approximately 80. Copper fell to $6.08 per pound ($13,404 per tonne LME), down 1.5%, pressured by the climbing dollar. Platinum dropped 1.7% to $1,500 and palladium eased 0.8% to $1,000, the latter sitting on psychological support. Grains staged a Friday bounce: wheat rose 1.6% to 593½¢, corn gained 0.8% to 446¢ and soybeans advanced 1.1% to 1,233¢, recovering some of Thursday's sharp losses. Cocoa edged higher to approximately $5,267 per tonne. The Washington Institute for Near East Policy counted 37 ship attacks in the Strait of Hormuz in October — the highest monthly total since the war began — even as crude prices stabilised after Trump's latest Iran remarks. Nickel eased to approximately $16,100 per tonne, tin slipped to $46,500 and zinc drifted to $3,700, all pressured by the firmer dollar. Newcastle coal held firm at approximately $143 per tonne. The November 27 gallium/germanium/antimony deadline is now 13 days away. Anthropic targets pricing its IPO on November 18 and trading on November 19 on the Nasdaq under ticker ANT — in what could be the largest AI company IPO in history.

watchItems.title: Bitcoin crashes below $70,000 on Friday the 13th — $1.3 billion liquidated in 24 hours
watchItems.text: Bitcoin plunged 5.1% to approximately $68,300 on Friday, crashing below both $70,000 and its 200-week moving average for the first time since August. The sell-off triggered over $1.3 billion in crypto futures liquidations within 24 hours, with $677 million on Bitcoin alone and $1.09 billion from long positions. The Fear and Greed Index collapsed to 20 — 'Extreme Fear' — its lowest reading since July. Ethereum fell 3.2% to approximately $1,930, slipping below $2,000 for the first time since August. US spot ETH ETFs have seen $695.9 million in net outflows over eight November sessions. MSCI's plan to remove Strategy (formerly MicroStrategy) from its global indexes could force index funds to sell shares of the largest corporate Bitcoin holder. Bitcoin has now fallen more than 21% year to date and is down over 30% from a year ago. Analysts cited three drivers converging: the Anthropic IPO reportedly draining liquid-asset allocations, the hawkish rates environment with yields above 5%, and Nvidia's ongoing leadership crisis undermining the AI-risk trade that previously supported crypto.

watchItems.title: Anthropic targets Nasdaq debut November 19 under ticker ANT — IPO reportedly 6x oversubscribed
watchItems.text: Anthropic is targeting pricing its IPO on November 18 and beginning trading on November 19 on the Nasdaq under ticker ANT. The IPO is reportedly six times oversubscribed and could raise as much as $64.4 billion, potentially valuing the company at up to $2 trillion — which would make it the largest AI company IPO in history. CoinDesk analysts noted that investors seeking allocations may be selling Bitcoin and other liquid risk assets to raise cash, contributing to Friday's crypto crash. The IPO timing coincides with a broader tech sell-off driven by Nvidia's leadership crisis and rising Treasury yields, though Anthropic appears to be benefiting from a 'flight to quality' narrative within the AI sector. The listing comes as CoreWeave's recent results eased some concerns about AI infrastructure spending.

watchItems.title: Hormuz ship attacks hit highest monthly total — 37 vessels struck in October
watchItems.text: The Washington Institute for Near East Policy counted 37 ships attacked in the Strait of Hormuz in October, the highest monthly total since the conflict began. Attacks showed little sign of slowing in November despite diplomatic gestures. On November 8, tanker strikes hit three vessels that Iranian state media said were using 'unauthorised routes.' Verified video showed a Navig8 tanker on fire off Oman, and satellite imagery confirmed oil slicks reaching Oman's and the UAE's shores. On November 7, US military aircraft disabled a cargo ship that had visited an Iranian port. On November 10, the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency reported another tanker struck northeast of Oman. The International Maritime Organization has confirmed 130 incidents since late February, with at least 25 seafarers killed. The UKMTO described Hormuz shipping as 'below normal, but not stalled.' Despite the escalation, crude prices remained range-bound as the market weighed supply risks against Trump's stated position of maintaining the naval blockade without seeking broader military action.

watchItems.title: China export-control deadline 13 days away — Anthropic IPO and APEC provide twin catalysts
watchItems.text: The November 27 deadline — when the suspension of China's export prohibition on gallium, germanium, antimony and superhard materials to the US expires — is now 13 days away. APEC leaders meet in Shenzhen November 18–19, providing a narrow diplomatic window for a possible Trump–Xi discussion on the deadline. The APEC meeting coincides with Anthropic's IPO pricing, adding an unusual alignment of technology and geopolitical catalysts in a single week. Gallium remains at approximately $2,100 per kilogram outside China versus $460 domestically — a 4.5x premium. Antimony holds at ¥93,500 per tonne in China. The November 10 lapse of Announcement No. 70 — covering rare earth equipment, technology and five additional rare earths — passed with no published extension. Alcoa's Wagerup gallium refinery in Western Australia has taken FID but is not yet producing.

desk.name: Gold
desk.m: Stabilized after 3-day plunge · PPI +6.5% YoY below 6.6% consensus · 10Y yield 5.15% · steepest weekly loss of 2026 · dollar index 103.4
desk.sum: Gold stabilized near $3,888 per ounce on Friday, up 0.3%, finding bargain-hunting support after Thursday's 2.8% plunge to near a one-year low. The October PPI came in at 0.3% month-over-month and 6.5% year-over-year — slightly below the 6.6% consensus — offering modest relief but failing to dent December rate-hike expectations. The 10-year Treasury yield rose to 5.15% and the dollar index climbed to 103.4. Despite Friday's bounce, gold posted its steepest weekly loss of 2026. CME FedWatch prices approximately 90% odds of a 25-basis-point hike at the December 8–9 FOMC. Oil's move above $95 on Trump's Iran comments adds inflation risk that could keep rates elevated for longer. Central bank buying at 675 tonnes year to date remains supportive but insufficient to offset the yield and dollar headwinds.

desk.name: Silver
desk.m: New one-year low · gold-silver ratio widened to ~80 · industrial demand weakening with AI sector · lost $50 level
desk.sum: Silver plunged 2.6% to $48.65 per ounce — a new one-year low — significantly underperforming gold's 0.3% gain. The gold-to-silver ratio widened to approximately 80 as silver's industrial-demand profile wilted alongside the AI sector sell-off. Silver has now lost more than 17% over the past month. The metal's dual precious-industrial role is working against it: rising yields reduce precious-metal appeal while weakening tech sentiment undermines industrial demand expectations. Solar panel demand provides a structural floor, but with the 10-year above 5.15%, the dollar at a 19-month high and the Nasdaq falling 0.9%, silver remains the most vulnerable precious metal.

desk.name: Oil
desk.m: WTI $88.30 · Trump: 'no deal needed' with Iran · 37 ship attacks in Hormuz in October · US crude stocks +4.7M bbl · weekly loss ~2.4%
desk.sum: Brent crude settled essentially flat at $95.84 per barrel on Friday, oscillating between geopolitical supply risk and demand concerns. Trump reiterated the US does not need a deal with Iran, maintaining the naval blockade posture. The Washington Institute counted 37 ship attacks in the Strait of Hormuz in October — the highest monthly total since the war began. WTI settled at $88.30, down 0.5%. US crude inventories rose 4.7 million barrels to 414.4 million for the week ended November 6, well above the expected 1.1 million barrel decline. Both benchmarks posted weekly declines of approximately 2.4%, on track for a second consecutive week of losses. UKMTO described Hormuz shipping as 'below normal, but not stalled.'

desk.name: Copper
desk.m: LME $13,404/t · weakest since early July · dollar at 103.4 19-month high · Yangshan premium still elevated
desk.sum: Copper fell 1.5% to $6.08 per pound ($13,404 per tonne LME 3M) on Friday — its weakest level since early July — as the dollar index climbed to 103.4 and Treasury yields held above 5.15%. The surging dollar makes dollar-denominated commodities more expensive for non-US buyers. The Yangshan copper import premium remains elevated, signalling continued Chinese physical demand, and SHFE stocks remain depleted. But the macro headwind from the hawkish rates environment is overpowering the constructive supply picture. Copper has now fallen more than 3% over two sessions since Thursday's 1.4% decline.

desk.name: Coal
desk.m: Up 40% YTD to ~$143–150 · LNG still elevated at ~$32 JKM · QatarEnergy FM through year-end · winter demand approaching
desk.sum: Newcastle coal held firm at approximately $143 per tonne, edging up modestly as the broader energy complex remained supported. Coal is up approximately 40% year to date as the Hormuz gas shock continues to revive thermal coal demand. QatarEnergy's force majeure extends through at least end-December 2026, keeping approximately 5 bcm of LNG supply offline. The IEA projects 2026 global LNG output will fall about 3%. EU storage sits below the five-year average ahead of winter. The combination of LNG supply tightness, winter demand approaching and geopolitical risk continues to provide a firm floor for seaborne coal pricing.

desk.name: Platinum
desk.m: Fell tracking broader precious metals selloff · industrial demand limits downside · PGM still outperforming gold relatively
desk.sum: Platinum fell 1.7% to approximately $1,500 per ounce on Friday, tracking silver's decline but outperforming on a relative basis. Platinum's industrial demand profile — hydrogen electrolysis, auto catalysts — continues to limit downside compared with pure precious metals. The WPIC supply deficit narrative remains constructive for the longer-term outlook. South African mine supply is constrained by ongoing power issues. With yields above 5.15% and the dollar at a 19-month high, the rate-sensitive precious metals complex remains under pressure, but platinum's industrial floor provides relative insulation compared with silver's 2.6% drop.

desk.name: Palladium
desk.m: Sitting on $1,000 psychological support · EV transition headwind persists · down less than 1% for the week
desk.sum: Palladium eased 0.8% to $1,000 per ounce on Friday, sitting directly on the psychologically important $1,000 support level. The metal is down less than 1% for the week, relatively contained compared with silver's steep decline. The structural headwind from the EV transition — battery EVs require no catalytic converter — remains the dominant longer-term dynamic. A decisive break below $1,000 would be technically significant and could trigger stop-loss selling. With yields above 5% and the dollar surging, the macro environment remains hostile to palladium's precious-metal profile.

desk.name: Hormuz Terminal
desk.m: 37 ships attacked in October (highest monthly total) · UKMTO: 'below normal but not stalled' · 130 incidents since Feb · 25 seafarers killed
desk.sum: The Strait of Hormuz risk remained critical with the Washington Institute counting 37 ship attacks in October — the highest monthly total since the conflict began. On November 8, tanker strikes hit three vessels that Iranian state media said were using 'unauthorised routes,' with verified video showing a Navig8 tanker on fire off Oman. Satellite imagery confirmed oil slicks reaching the shores of Oman and the UAE. On November 10, UKMTO reported another tanker struck northeast of Oman. The International Maritime Organization has confirmed 130 incidents since late February, with at least 25 seafarers killed. UKMTO described Hormuz shipping as 'below normal, but not stalled.' US forces continue the naval blockade — on November 7, a US aircraft disabled a cargo ship that visited an Iranian port. Despite the escalation, crude prices remained range-bound as markets focus on the blockade posture rather than broader military action.

desk.name: Corn
desk.m: Rebounded from Thursday's selloff · dollar headwind persists · WASDE tighter balance sheets still supportive · South American planting favourable
desk.sum: December corn rose 3½ cents to 446¢ per bushel on Friday, recovering part of Thursday's 5½-cent selloff as grains staged a broad Friday bounce. The rebound came despite the dollar index climbing to 103.4 — a 19-month high — suggesting end-of-week short-covering. The USDA's tighter balance sheet from last week's WASDE report continues to provide structural support, with the November yield cut (179.6 bushels per acre) below all analyst estimates. South American planting continues under generally favourable conditions. The weekly performance remains negative despite Friday's bounce, with the hawkish rates environment and strong dollar capping upside potential for US grain export competitiveness.

desk.name: Wheat
desk.m: Best performer among grains · recovered from Thursday's reversal below 600¢ · SovEcon: Russian exports 36 mmt vs USDA 39 mmt
desk.sum: December wheat rose 9¼ cents to 593½¢ per bushel on Friday — the best performer among grains on the day — recovering a significant portion of Thursday's 15¼-cent selloff. The rebound brought wheat back within range of the 600¢ level that was briefly breached on Wednesday. SovEcon's cut of its Russian wheat export estimate to 36 million tonnes (below the USDA's 39 million tonne forecast) remains a medium-term bullish factor. The Abu Dhabi grain corridor talks remain a key potential bearish catalyst if they restart stalled Black Sea shipments. Despite Friday's bounce, wheat posted a weekly loss as the macro-driven selling on Wednesday and Thursday overwhelmed the WASDE-driven rally.

desk.name: Soybean
desk.m: January front-month $12.33 · rebounded from Thursday · stronger dollar still weighing on export competitiveness
desk.sum: January soybeans rose 14 cents to $12.33 per bushel (1,233¢) on Friday, bouncing back from Thursday's 11¾-cent decline. The rebound was supported by end-of-week short-covering despite the dollar index climbing to 103.4. South American supplies remain more competitive than US offerings at current exchange rates, and Chinese buying interest is still muted. The USDA's tighter balance sheet from the WASDE report provides a structural floor. Soybeans outperformed corn on the day, recovering all of Thursday's losses. The soybean ETF proxy (SOYB) rose 0.97%.

desk.name: Cryptocurrencies
desk.m: ETH $1,930 · crashed below $70K and 200-week MA · $1.3B liquidations · Fear & Greed at 20 'Extreme Fear' · Anthropic IPO draining liquidity
desk.sum: Bitcoin crashed below $70,000 on Friday the 13th, plunging 5.1% to approximately $68,300 — its weakest level since August and below the 200-week moving average for the first time. Over $1.3 billion in crypto futures were liquidated within 24 hours, with $677 million on Bitcoin and $1.09 billion from longs. The Fear and Greed Index collapsed to 20 — 'Extreme Fear.' Ethereum fell 3.2% to $1,930, slipping below $2,000 for the first time since August; US spot ETH ETFs have seen $695.9 million in net outflows across eight November sessions. Analysts cited three converging headwinds: the Anthropic IPO — reportedly six times oversubscribed — draining liquid-asset allocations, Treasury yields above 5% raising opportunity costs, and the Nvidia leadership crisis undermining the AI-risk trade. Bitcoin dominance is at 60.2%. MSCI's plan to remove Strategy from global indexes adds further selling pressure on the largest corporate BTC holder.

desk.name: LNG
desk.m: JKM ~$32 · TTF fell ~18% to $28/MMBtu · HH $3.00 · QatarEnergy FM through year-end · winter demand approaching
desk.sum: Asian LNG spot (JKM) trades near $32 per MMBtu, holding steady as winter demand approaches. The November 9 weekly update showed JKM briefly dipping to the low $32s before stabilizing. European TTF fell significantly to approximately $28 per MMBtu on easing near-term supply concerns, while Henry Hub rose modestly to $3.00. QatarEnergy's force majeure extends through at least end-December 2026, keeping approximately 5 bcm of supply offline. The IEA projects 2026 global LNG output will fall about 3% — the steepest annual drop on record. EU storage sits below the five-year average ahead of winter. Oil remaining above $95 indirectly supports LNG pricing through energy-complex correlation.

desk.name: Sulfur
desk.m: FOB Kuwait ~$765 · 37 ship attacks in Hormuz in Oct reduce supply restart odds · 13 days to Nov 27 deadline
desk.sum: Sulfur remains elevated at approximately $1,200 per tonne CFR Southeast Asia. The Washington Institute's count of 37 ship attacks in the Strait of Hormuz in October — the highest monthly total since the conflict began — further reduces the near-term probability of Middle Eastern supply resumption. Oil slicks from tanker fires have reached the shores of Oman and the UAE. FOB Kuwait holds near $765 (KPC). Chinese domestic sulfur holds near 7,200 yuan per tonne. The November 27 export-control deadline is now 13 days away. Trump's reiterated stance that Washington does not need a deal with Iran signals a continued hardline posture.

desk.name: Potash
desk.m: BPC India $383 CFR · China benchmark ~$348 · grain rebound Friday modestly supportive · WASDE tighter balance sheets underpin
desk.sum: Muriate of potash (MOP) CFR Brazil holds at approximately $358 per tonne. BPC's India contract remains approximately $25 above China's 2026 benchmark at $383 per tonne CFR. Friday's grain rebound — wheat up 1.6%, soybeans up 1.1% — modestly improved fertiliser sentiment after Thursday's sharp sell-off, though the weekly performance remains negative for grains. The underlying WASDE-driven tighter grain balance sheets remain supportive for the 2027 planting season. Belarus and Russia still account for about 40% of global supply despite Western sanctions.
desk.src: World Bank · Argus Media · SP Angel

desk.name: Antimony
desk.m: 13 days to Nov 27 deadline · Rotterdam $18,300–19,000/t · APEC Nov 18–19 coincides with Anthropic IPO pricing
desk.sum: Chinese antimony (#1 ingot) holds near 93,500 yuan per tonne. Overseas antimony sits at approximately $18,300–19,000 per tonne in Rotterdam. The critical near-term catalyst remains the November 27 deadline — now 13 days away — when the suspension of China's export prohibition on antimony (and gallium, germanium, superhard materials) to the US expires. APEC leaders meet in Shenzhen November 18–19, coinciding with Anthropic's IPO pricing — an unusual alignment of geopolitical and technology catalysts. The November 10 lapse of Announcement No. 70 has already passed with no published extension.

desk.name: Gallium & Germanium
desk.m: Up >130% since early 2025 · 13 days to Nov 27 deadline · China domestic Ga $460/kg · Ge $4,625/kg · Alcoa Wagerup FID but not producing
desk.sum: Gallium holds near $2,100 per kilogram outside China, with Chinese domestic gallium at approximately $460 per kilogram — a roughly 4.5x premium for ex-China supply. Germanium in China sits at approximately $4,625 per kilogram. The November 27 deadline is now 13 days away. APEC in Shenzhen November 18–19 provides the last major diplomatic window before the deadline, coinciding with Anthropic's IPO pricing on November 18. Alcoa's Wagerup gallium refinery in Western Australia has taken FID but is not yet producing. China produces about 98% of global gallium. The approaching deadline adds urgency to any potential Trump–Xi discussions at APEC.

desk.name: Vanadium
desk.m: Firmer at $5.30 vs recent $5.02 · VRFB adoption timeline uncertain · China-Russia-SA control 90%+ supply
desk.sum: Vanadium pentoxide (V₂O₅) holds at approximately $5.30 per pound in Europe, up from recent levels near $5.02. The modest recovery reflects stabilisation in steel demand rather than a structural shift. The long-term bull case rests on vanadium redox flow batteries (VRFBs) for grid-scale energy storage, but large-scale adoption timing remains uncertain. China, Russia and South Africa control over 90% of supply. The November 27 export-control deadline could impact vanadium indirectly if superhard materials restrictions affect adjacent supply chains.

desk.name: Cocoa
desk.m: Continued rebound from 4-month lows · Sodexam: Ivory Coast output may fall 21–25% · El Niño 'exceptionally strong' · ICE inventories at 2.5-year high
desk.sum: ICE cocoa edged higher to approximately $5,267 per tonne on Friday, continuing its recovery from four-month lows touched earlier in the week. Ivory Coast's national weather agency Sodexam projected 2026/27 output could drop 21–25% due to an 'exceptionally strong El Niño event' that is shortening the rainy season. Reuters had earlier projected the mid-crop could fall 42–50% to 300,000–350,000 tonnes. Harmattan wind risk in December–January adds further supply concern. ICE warehouse inventories remain elevated at a 2.5-year high, capping the near-term recovery. Heavy rains reportedly damaged roads in key growing regions, slowing bean deliveries to collection centres.

desk.name: Cobalt
desk.m: Glencore wins $900M US stockpile contract · Rotterdam standard-grade $17–18/lb · NMC-to-LFP shift continues
desk.sum: Cobalt holds near $33,525 per tonne, under continued pressure. Glencore reportedly won a US government contract to supply up to $900 million of cobalt over five years for strategic stockpiles, though volumes and pricing remain unconfirmed. Rotterdam standard-grade cobalt metal sits at $17–18 per pound, down from $21–22 per pound in early October. The DRC maintains export quotas of 96,600 tonnes per year through 2027. The EV battery chemistry shift from NMC to LFP continues to structurally reduce cobalt intensity. Antaike expects recycled cobalt supply to rise 26% to 50,000 tonnes this year.
desk.src: Trading Economics · Argus Media · SP Angel

desk.name: Lithium
desk.m: Near one-year low · SMM: Chinese stockpile 175k t · Mineral Resources restarts Bald Hill · Goldman: 444k t global surplus by 2028
desk.sum: Chinese lithium carbonate futures hover near ¥90,650 per tonne, close to a one-year low. SMM's revised inventory estimate of 175,000 tonnes in Chinese stockpiles — roughly double the earlier figure — remains a bearish overhang for supply-demand balance. Mineral Resources has restarted the Bald Hill mine after an 18-month suspension, and Core Lithium has restarted Finniss. The EU's plan to cap Chinese EV imports at 350,000 units per year adds a demand headwind. Goldman Sachs projects a 444,000-tonne global surplus by 2028. Lithium's inability to rally despite the broader commodity complex finding some support on Friday underscores the structural oversupply challenge.

desk.name: Rubber
desk.m: $2.55/kg · SE Asia supply tight · fungal blight ongoing · oil above $95 supports synthetic rubber costs
desk.sum: Natural rubber (RSS3) trades near $2,550 per tonne ($2.55/kg), range-bound. Southeast Asian supply remains tight with Thailand, Indonesia and Malaysia — producing 70% of global latex — still affected by Pestalotiopsis fungal leaf blight. Oil remaining above $95 modestly supports synthetic rubber costs, which indirectly benefits natural rubber pricing. Auto-sector demand remains solid, supported by replacement-tyre cycles. The stronger dollar at a 19-month high is a headwind for dollar-denominated commodities.

desk.name: Uranium
desk.m: Futures above $91 · long-term contracts near $99/lb approaching $100 · IAEA raises nuclear capacity outlook · 78 reactors under construction
desk.sum: Uranium spot holds at approximately $91 per pound U₃O₈, with futures above $91 as of mid-November. Long-term contract prices continue climbing near record US levels of $99 per pound — approaching the $100 milestone. The IAEA raised its outlook for global nuclear capacity over the next two decades and counts 78 reactors under construction worldwide. Kazatomprom reported 25% year-over-year growth in sales turnover for the September quarter. Delays at Kazatomprom's TQZ sulphuric acid plant limit leaching capacity. AI data-centre power demand remains a structural driver, with Meta, Amazon and Microsoft having signed nuclear power agreements. Italy has expressed interest in a legal framework to restore nuclear power.

desk.name: Rare Earths
desk.m: China domestic NdPr declining · ex-China premiums up to 10x · LS Cable/KMMI $490M to reduce China reliance · Lynas maintenance
desk.sum: Neodymium-praseodymium (NdPr) oxide trades near $72 per kilogram domestically in China, softening, while ex-China FOB prices remain elevated at $109–121 per kilogram. Western buyers face premiums of up to 10x Chinese prices for heavy rare earths. LS Cable & System and KMMI committed $490 million to reduce reliance on Chinese rare earth magnets. Lynas' Malaysian plant maintenance shutdown continues, and its Kalgoorlie plant is halted for power grid upgrades. China Rare Earth Group has ordered tighter executive oversight of its heavy rare earth supply chain. The November 27 deadline is now 13 days away.
desk.src: SMM · Rare Earth Exchanges · SP Angel

desk.name: Manganese
desk.m: South Africa 37% · Gabon 18% · miners holding firm pricing stance · CIF China flat
desk.sum: Manganese ore (44% Mn content) trades near $4.40 per dry metric tonne unit CIF China, flat. Miners are holding a firm pricing stance, with Comilog (Gabonese lumps) at $4.50 per mtu and Consolidated Minerals (Australian 46% lumps) at $4.80 per mtu for recent shipments. South Africa supplies about 37% of global ore and Gabon 18%. Steel production consumes 90% of manganese demand. The forward cost picture provides support, but soft downstream consumption limits gains.

desk.name: Nickel
desk.m: Eased on dollar strength · Indonesia RKAB quota tightening provides support · surplus persists
desk.sum: LME nickel eased to approximately $16,100 per tonne on Friday, down 0.8%, as the dollar index climbed to 103.4. Indonesia's potential tightening of RKAB mining quotas provides a modest floor, but the global nickel surplus persists as Indonesian NPI and HPAL expansions continue. The 10-year yield above 5.15% and the dollar at a 19-month high remain headwinds for industrial metals. Nickel has fallen more than 1% for the week as the macro environment continues to pressure base metals despite constructive supply-side developments.

desk.name: Tin
desk.m: Modest decline · LME inventories near 4,000 mt · Myanmar ban still constraining supply · best relative performer among base metals this week
desk.sum: LME tin eased to approximately $46,500 per tonne on Friday, down 0.3%, modestly outperforming the broader base metals complex. LME inventory holds near 4,000 mt — low for the year — providing a floor. Structural supply constraints persist from Myanmar's Wa State mining ban and Indonesian export licensing tightness. Tin's relative outperformance on a day when copper fell 1.5% and zinc dropped 0.7% reflects its tighter fundamental supply position. The cancelled warrants ratio near 19.5% signals further drawdowns ahead.

desk.name: Zinc
desk.m: TCs deeply negative · LME stocks fell to ~142,625 mt · dollar pressure persistent · smelter curtailments continue
desk.sum: LME zinc eased to approximately $3,700 per tonne on Friday, down 0.7%, with the dollar at a 19-month high continuing to weigh on the market. LME inventories fell 950 tonnes to 142,625 mt, continuing the drawdown trend. Treatment charges remain deeply negative, forcing continued smelter curtailments. SMM described off-season demand as weak across Chinese hubs, though limited supply in some regions supported premiums. The structural supply deficit that has driven zinc higher through 2026 remains intact, but the combination of yields above 5%, dollar surge and soft downstream consumption is capping near-term upside.

desk.name: Tungsten
desk.m: Rotterdam APT $2,725 · China FOB $1,845 · Western ~3.5x China · 13 days to Nov 27 deadline
desk.sum: European tungsten APT trades at $2,725 per mtu in Rotterdam, while Chinese FOB sits at $1,845 per mtu. Western prices remain roughly 3.5 times Chinese domestic levels. Chongyi tungsten enterprises raised long-term contract prices for the first half of November, reflecting upstream tightness. The market continues to reflect the fragmentation created by China's export controls on tungsten processing technology. The November 27 deadline for the US-specific ban is now 13 days away. APEC in Shenzhen November 18–19 provides a diplomatic window, coinciding with Anthropic's IPO pricing.

desk.name: Helium
desk.m: Up 358% YTD · Ras Laffan repair 3–5 years · 37 Hormuz attacks in Oct · Trump: 'no deal needed' with Iran
desk.sum: Grade-A helium trades near $390 per thousand cubic feet, at critical levels. The Washington Institute's count of 37 Hormuz ship attacks in October — the highest monthly total — and Trump's reiterated stance that Washington does not need a deal with Iran further extend the timeline for any comprehensive conflict resolution and potential Ras Laffan facility repairs, currently estimated at 3–5 years. Qatar and the US together supply about 81% of global helium. Russia's export controls extend through 2027. Commercial inventories remain at their lowest since 2008. Semiconductor fabs, MRI machines and space launch consume most demand.

desk.name: Phosphate
desk.m: OCP 30% global · DAP $560/t · sulfur cost surge pressuring economics · grain rebound modestly supportive
desk.sum: Phosphate rock trades near $120 per tonne FOB Morocco, with Morocco's OCP Group controlling about 30% of global trade. DAP prices sit near $560 per tonne CFR India. The sulfur price surge continues to pressure phosphate production economics. Friday's grain rebound — wheat up 1.6%, corn up 0.8% — modestly improved the near-term fertiliser demand outlook after Thursday's sell-off. The underlying WASDE-driven tighter balance sheets remain supportive heading into the 2027 planting season. The 37 Hormuz attacks in October further reduce the probability of Middle Eastern sulfur supply normalising.
